name: Windowing and Watermarks
intent: Group an unbounded stream into finite windows by when events happened, and use a watermark to decide when a window is complete enough to emit.
scenario: An ad platform counts clicks per 10-second window by event time. Phones sometimes go through a tunnel and upload clicks late, so events arrive out of order (event times 12, 8, 5, 14, 22, 11, 25, 9). A watermark of newest event time minus 5 seconds decides when a window fires; the click at time 9 that arrives after 25 misses its window.
problem: A stream never ends, so an aggregate such as count per minute needs a boundary. Processing time (the clock of the machine) is easy but gives wrong answers when events are delayed or replayed: a backfill would put a week of clicks into one minute. Event time is correct but then the operator never knows whether all events for a window have arrived. Waiting forever is not an option, firing too early gives wrong numbers, and waiting too long makes the result slow and the state huge.

howItWorks.title: Assign each event to a window by its event time
howItWorks.text: Tumbling windows are fixed and do not overlap (start = floor(t / size) * size). Sliding (hopping) windows overlap, so one event lands in size / slide windows. Session windows have no fixed size: they grow while events keep arriving within a gap, and close after a gap of inactivity. The event time is a timestamp in the record, taken when the thing happened, not when the server saw it.

howItWorks.title: Track a watermark: a claim about event-time progress
howItWorks.text: A watermark W(t) says no more events with event time at or below t are expected. The common generator is bounded out-of-orderness: watermark = max event time seen minus a fixed delay. It only moves forward. With several input partitions, an operator uses the minimum watermark over its inputs, so one idle or slow partition holds everything back unless it is marked idle.

howItWorks.title: Fire the window when the watermark passes its end
howItWorks.text: Open windows keep their partial aggregate in state. When the watermark reaches a window's end, the operator emits the result and normally discards the state. The delay is therefore the trade-off knob: a larger delay captures more late events but delays every result by that amount and holds more windows open.

howItWorks.title: Decide what happens to late events
howItWorks.text: An event whose window has already fired is late. Options: drop it (the default in most engines, ideally counted in a metric), send it to a side output (a separate stream of late events) for repair later, or keep the window state for an allowed-lateness period (Flink allowedLateness, Beam allowed lateness) and emit an updated, corrected result for each late event, which downstream consumers must handle as an update.

howItWorks.title: Choose triggers and handle the idle source problem
howItWorks.text: Triggers decide when to emit: at the watermark (default), early speculative results every N seconds or elements, and late results after the watermark. Beam calls this the what, where, when and how of a pipeline. If a source stops sending, its watermark stalls and no window closes, so engines support idleness timeouts that exclude a silent input from the minimum.

pros: Results depend on when events happened, so replays, backfills and delayed uploads give the same answer as live processing
A tunable trade-off between completeness and latency instead of an implicit one
Bounded state: finished windows are dropped instead of growing forever
Late data can be made visible (side output, metrics, updates) rather than silently mixed in
cons: The watermark is a heuristic: for most real sources there is no guarantee that nothing older will arrive
Every result is delayed by at least the watermark delay, so it is not for sub-second dashboards that must be exact
Late-data handling adds complexity: updates, retractions and idempotent sinks
Hard to test and debug: behaviour depends on event time, parallelism and arrival order
A stalled partition or idle source can freeze all output
whenToUse: Aggregates over a stream where the answer must match event time: billing, ad clicks, fraud counts, SLO metrics
Sources with real disorder: mobile clients, multi-partition topics, multiple producers, replays and backfills
Pipelines that must give the same result when reprocessed from the log as when run live
whenNotToUse: When processing time is what you want: monitoring the load on your own system right now
When a nightly batch over the finished day is simple and the latency is acceptable; a batch job sees all the data and needs no watermark
When the source is strictly ordered with negligible delay, as with one partition and a single writer; event-time windows still work but the delay can be near zero
When you need exact results at any cost and cannot tolerate dropped or corrected late data; then keep the raw events and recompute
pitfalls: Using processing time by accident (default in some APIs), so a restart or backlog lands hours of events in one window
A watermark delay set from the average lateness instead of a high percentile, which drops the long tail every day
One idle Kafka partition (for example a topic with 12 partitions and 8 producers) pins the minimum watermark and no window ever fires
Event timestamps from client clocks that are wrong by minutes or in the future: one future event pushes the watermark ahead and makes everything after it late
Silently dropping late events with no metric, so the totals are quietly low
Allowed lateness without an idempotent or upserting sink, which double counts when the updated window result is emitted again

roles.label: Event source
roles.description: Phones and servers that stamp each click with the event time when it happened.

roles.label: Event log
roles.description: A partitioned log such as Kafka that delivers events in arrival order, which is not event-time order.

roles.label: Window operator
roles.description: Holds a partial count per open window and fires it when the watermark passes the window end.

roles.label: Watermark
roles.description: Tracks the newest event time minus the allowed delay and claims how far event time has progressed.

roles.label: Sink
roles.description: Receives the emitted window results, for example a dashboard table or a billing store.

quiz.question: A job counts clicks per minute using processing time. After a 6-hour outage it replays the backlog and one minute's window shows the clicks of 6 hours. What is the best fix?
options: Use shorter windows such as 10 seconds
Add more parallel instances so the backlog drains faster
Use sliding windows with a 10 second slide
Window by event time with a watermark
quiz.explanation: Processing time assigns events to the clock at replay, so a backlog collapses into a few windows. Event time puts each click in the minute it happened, so replays match live results. Window size or parallelism does not change this.

quiz.question: A team sees 3% of events dropped as late and raises the watermark delay from 5 seconds to 10 minutes. What is the main cost?
options: Out-of-order events are dropped instead of being counted
Every result comes about 10 minutes later, with more windows open
None, because the delay only affects events that were late
Counts quietly turn into processing-time counts
quiz.explanation: The watermark delay trades completeness for latency: a window fires only when the watermark passes its end, so all results wait and more state is held. The delay does not change which events are on time, only how long the job waits for them.

quiz.question: A topic has 12 partitions but only 8 producers, so 4 partitions never receive data. Since the job started, no window has ever fired. What is the cause and fix?
options: The watermark delay is too small, so raise it
Allowed lateness is off, so switch it on
Idle partitions pin the minimum watermark, so set an idleness timeout
The windows are too large, so make them shorter
quiz.explanation: With several inputs the operator uses the minimum watermark, and a silent partition never advances. An idleness timeout excludes it. A larger delay or lateness shifts when windows fire but cannot move a stalled watermark.
